descs.t: Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens endorsed Republican Mike Rogers over Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in the Michigan Senate race, and on Election Day some lifelong Democrats told CNN and ABC they followed her. Other voters, including one Republican, said they went the other way. We walk through the endorsement, the voters' own words and what it means for the race.

Haley Stevens' endorsement of Mike Rogers split Michigan Democrats on Election Day. Senator John Fetterman called Abdul El-Sayed a communist, Barack Obama made a last-minute push for him, and Bernie Sanders says AIPAC spent heavily against him. We break down why the crossover vote matters and who it helps.

A sitting Democrat crossed party lines to back Mike Rogers, and Michigan Democrats are telling reporters they did the same because they see Abdul El-Sayed as too far left. We look at why voters say they broke with their party and what the backlash against Haley Stevens says about the left.

intro.plain: It's Election Day in Michigan, and the Senate race just got strange. Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens endorsed the Republican, Mike Rogers, over Abdul El-Sayed, and now lifelong Democrats are telling CNN they followed her. Others went the other way. So tell me in the chat: is crossing party lines an act of courage or betrayal?
intro.mid: Michigan is voting today and the Democratic base is split. Haley Stevens backed Mike Rogers, Fetterman called Abdul El-Sayed a communist, and Obama made a last-minute push for him. Voters on camera say they're crossing over. This is the race to watch tonight. Chat, if you're in Michigan, who did you vote for and why?
intro.bold: A sitting Democrat just told her own voters to back the Republican, and some of them listened. Haley Stevens endorsed Mike Rogers, and Michigan Democrats are going on CNN saying El-Sayed is too far left for them. Her critics call it treachery. I think she showed spine. Chat, would you cross party lines to stop a candidate you see as dangerous?

hook.plain: On Election Day, lifelong Michigan Democrats told reporters they voted Republican for the first time, after Haley Stevens endorsed Mike Rogers. Here is what they said and why it matters for the Senate race.
hook.mid: A Democrat endorsed the Republican, and her voters followed. Haley Stevens backed Mike Rogers over Abdul El-Sayed, and the crossover vote is now the story of the night. Here is why.
hook.bold: Lifelong Democrats, voting Republican for the first time, saying their own candidate is too far left. That is Michigan today. Here is how Haley Stevens broke the party line.

descs.t: On Election Day, President Trump posted a wave of endorsements for America First candidates, from Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton to Vivek Ramaswamy in Ohio, Byron Donalds in Florida, Andy Biggs in Arizona and Michael Whatley in North Carolina. We go through who he backed and which races they are in.

Trump used Election Day to put his name behind candidates for governor in Ohio, Florida, New York, Arizona and Tennessee, plus Senate and House races in North Carolina, Texas and Wisconsin. We look at what the list says about the party he wants after the midterms.

Trump is going all in on Election Day, endorsing Ken Paxton, Vivek Ramaswamy, Byron Donalds, Marsha Blackburn and more as America First Patriots. We walk through the races where his endorsement is on the line tonight and what a win or a loss would mean for his movement.

intro.plain: Polls are open and President Trump has been posting endorsements all day. Ken Paxton in Texas, Vivek Ramaswamy for governor of Ohio, Byron Donalds in Florida, Andy Biggs in Arizona, Marsha Blackburn in Tennessee. Tonight we find out how much his name still moves voters. Chat, which of these races are you watching most closely?
intro.mid: Trump is using Election Day to pick his governors. Ramaswamy in Ohio, Donalds in Florida, Blakeman in New York, Biggs in Arizona, Blackburn in Tennessee, all called America First Patriots. This is him shaping the party for after the midterms. Chat, which of his picks do you think is most at risk tonight?
intro.bold: Trump just went all in. Endorsement after endorsement on Election Day: Paxton, Ramaswamy, Donalds, Biggs, Blackburn, Whatley. His name is on the ballot in all of these races in everything but print. If they win, his movement owns the party. If they lose, it's on him. Chat, is this a power move or a gamble?

hook.plain: On Election Day, President Trump endorsed candidates from Texas to Arizona to North Carolina. Here is who he backed, which races they are in, and why it matters tonight.
hook.mid: Ohio, Florida, New York, Arizona, Tennessee. Trump picked a governor in every one of them today. Here is the bench he is building and what it says about his party.
hook.bold: Trump is putting his name behind a wave of America First candidates as the polls open. Tonight decides whether that name still wins. Here are the races to watch.

Tucker Carlson is warning that Trump may use a nuclear weapon on the Islamic Republic's Pickaxe Mountain site, and regime state TV has aired instructions on surviving a nuclear strike. Critics like Nick Fuentes call Tucker's warning fearmongering. We break down what is known and what is claim.

Trump has put Pickaxe Mountain, the regime's buried nuclear site, on notice, and the Islamic Republic is now telling its own people how to survive a nuclear strike. We look at Tucker Carlson's alarm, what Trump actually said, and why this site matters so much to the regime.

descs.t: The Supreme Court rejected the Trump administration's emergency request to make California set aside roughly 20,000 disputed mail ballots ahead of the midterms, AP and CBS News report. We go through what was asked, what the court did and what the Ninth Circuit ruled after.

Trump's last-ditch push to set aside about 20,000 California mail ballots failed at the Supreme Court, and Governor Gavin Newsom warned that anyone who tampers with ballots will be prosecuted. We look at what the ruling means for California's count and for Election Day disputes elsewhere.

Trump took a fight over 20,000 California mail ballots all the way to the Supreme Court and lost, while Gavin Newsom fired back with threats of prosecution. We break down the ballot war behind today's vote and what both sides are claiming.

intro.plain: Before the polls even closed, the Supreme Court weighed in. It rejected the Trump administration's request to make California set aside about 20,000 disputed mail ballots. Gavin Newsom is now warning anyone who interferes will be prosecuted. Chat, do you think this was the right call by the court?
intro.mid: Trump lost at the Supreme Court on the eve of the midterms. The administration wanted California to set aside roughly 20,000 mail ballots. The court said no, the Ninth Circuit ruled late at night, and Newsom is threatening prosecution. This fight is not over. Chat, do you expect more ballot cases after tonight?
intro.bold: A ballot war just broke out over California. Trump wanted about 20,000 mail ballots set aside, the Supreme Court shut him down, and Newsom is promising to prosecute anyone who touches the count. Both sides say they are protecting the vote. Chat, who do you trust more on election security here?

hook.plain: The Supreme Court has rejected the Trump administration's request to set aside about 20,000 California mail ballots. Here is what was asked, and what the court decided.
hook.mid: Hours before the midterms, Trump lost a ballot fight at the Supreme Court. Here is why the court would not touch California's disputed mail ballots.
hook.bold: Twenty thousand mail ballots, a Supreme Court no, and Gavin Newsom threatening prosecution. Here is the ballot war behind today's vote.

descs.t: President Trump announced on Fox News that the US will stop roughly $4 billion in annual military aid to Israel at the end of the year, saying he and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu made a deal. We go through what Trump said, when it takes effect and how Israel responded.

Trump says Netanyahu raised the issue and the two agreed to end about $4 billion a year in US military aid to Israel. Israeli broadcaster Kan reports Israel was caught off guard by the announcement. We look at the competing accounts and the reaction from MTG, Glenn Greenwald and the silence from AIPAC.

On Election Day, Trump pulled the plug on $4 billion a year in military aid to Israel and said Netanyahu agreed to it. We look at what it means for a free nation under attack, whether Israel can stand on its own, and why the announcement landed today.

intro.plain: Huge announcement this morning. Trump went on Fox News and said the US will stop giving Israel about $4 billion a year in military aid, starting at the end of the year. He says he and Netanyahu made a deal. Israeli media say Israel was caught off guard. Chat, is this good or bad for Israel?
intro.mid: Trump says he and Netanyahu made a deal to end $4 billion a year in US military aid to Israel, and that Netanyahu raised it. But Israeli broadcaster Kan reports Israel was blindsided. Two very different stories, on Election Day. Chat, whose account do you believe here?
intro.bold: Trump just pulled the plug on $4 billion a year for Israel, live on Fox News, on Election Day. He says Netanyahu agreed. Israel says it was blindsided. Israel is fighting for its life against the Islamic Republic and its proxies. Chat, can Israel stand on its own, and should it have to?

hook.plain: President Trump says the US will stop roughly $4 billion a year in military aid to Israel. Here is what he announced, when it starts, and how Israel responded.
hook.mid: Trump says Netanyahu asked to end US military aid. Israel says it was blindsided. Here is the deal, and the two stories about it.

descs.t: The US carried out what officials call defensive strikes on Qeshm Island the night before the midterm elections, Reuters and the WSJ report. Trump says the targets included an anti-aircraft facility the Islamic Republic had built. We go through what was hit and what officials and Trump have said.

US officials describe last night's strikes on Qeshm Island as defensive, and Trump says the Islamic Republic has no anti-aircraft left after the US took out a facility it had built. We look at why the strikes were framed as defensive and why they came on the eve of the midterms.

The Islamic Republic rebuilt an anti-aircraft facility on Qeshm Island, and the US took it out overnight. Trump says the regime has no anti-aircraft left. We look at what these strikes show about how exposed the regime has become.

intro.plain: Overnight, the US carried out strikes on Qeshm Island, and officials are calling them defensive. Trump says the target was an anti-aircraft facility the Islamic Republic had built. This came the night before the midterms. Chat, what do you think the US is trying to prevent here?
intro.mid: The US hit Qeshm Island last night, and officials call it defensive. Trump says the regime has no anti-aircraft left after the US took some out. Some critics online are tying the timing to the midterms. Chat, is this a one-off or the start of something bigger?
intro.bold: The Islamic Republic built itself a new anti-aircraft facility on Qeshm Island, and the US took it out overnight. Trump says the regime has no anti-aircraft left. A regime that cannot protect its own skies is a regime in trouble. Chat, how much longer can it hold on?
